02／11
PLAY
ＰＬＡＹ　再生
Press it. What comes back is almost your song.

VHS Vibes makes clean audio sound like it lived on a video cassette. Put it on a track and the pitch starts to swim, the highs soften, the hiss comes up in the quiet parts and, if you let it, the machine loses the tape for a moment and finds it again.

  • An insert effect, stereo in, stereo out, for Akai MPC standalone hardware.
  • 60 controls on 5 pages, 54 built-in programs.
  • A hot pink cassette on the MPC's screen, with reels that turn when sound passes. With Visual Vibes on, the picture shows what the sound is doing.
  • The plugin synthesizes every noise: no samples, nothing to load.
  • Much of it comes from published figures: the VHS linear track and its head out of line (Azimuth), the FM sound of the Hi-Fi track, the noise reduction of early stereo decks, four period microphones and the record level control of an early VHS deck. With Hysteresis on, the VHS tape records through a Preisach model of how tape records. The chapter ＩＮＳＩＤＥ　ＴＨＥ　ＭＡＣＨＩＮＥ opens them all up.
  • This manual describes version 1.8.0.
03／11
INSERT
ＩＮＳＥＲＴ　ＴＡＰＥ　挿入
The machine takes the tape out of your hand. It has done this before.

Install

VHS Vibes needs MPC OS 3.10.1 or later.

  1. Take the zip from the Releases page of the project: https://github.com/anthonytheinventor/vhs-vibes/releases
  2. Copy the folder anthonytheinventor - VST - VHS Vibes into a folder named VST2 Plugins at the top of a USB drive, an SD card or the MPC's internal drive.
  3. On the MPC open Preferences > Enhancements (Beta) and switch on both Enable Enhancements and External Plugin Support.
  4. Restart the MPC.
  5. VHS Vibes is in the plugin browser under External Plugins.

INSTALL.txt in the zip has the same steps.

First sound

  1. Load VHS Vibes as an insert effect on a track and play something through it.
  2. It opens on Home Recording: a family tape in good shape, with gentle wobble, some hiss and a level control that rides a little.
  3. You hear hiss and hum even when nothing plays. That is the tape. The Power switch on the NOISE page turns it off.
  4. Step through the programs to hear what the machine can do. The chapter ＴＡＰＥＳ　ＩＮ　ＴＨＥ　ＢＯＸ lists them.
  5. To build a sound from scratch, choose Init: a blank tape that passes the sound through unchanged. Then turn up one thing at a time.
  6. If the effect is too much, turn Mix down on the TAPE page to let the untouched input back in, or start from Subtle Glue.

ＳＣＲＥＥＮ　スクリーン

The cassette

Every page is the same cassette with a different set of controls on its face. The screens in this manual show every control at its default.

There are three kinds of control:

ON SCREENWHAT IT ISHOW IT READS
A knob with a window under itA continuous valueThe window shows the value with its unit, for example 25 % or 9.0 kHz.
A pill that says ON or OFFA switchLit pink when on.
Two, three or four buttonsA selectorThe lit button is the current choice.

The name printed above a control is sometimes shorter than the name the MPC uses for it elsewhere, for example in automation: the knob printed RATE in the FLUTTER block is the parameter Flut Rate. This manual gives both.

Type on the TAPE page recolors the controls it works with. On VHS they turn mint green, on Hi-Fi sunset orange, on whichever page they are, and the lit Type button wears the same shade. The Azimuth knob and the Hysteresis switch on the DECK page appear only while Type is VHS.

The Q-Links

Each block of four controls is one Q-Link group. Touch a control and the four Q-Link knobs follow its block, left to right. The MPC marks the selected block with a Q in its top left corner, which is why the block titles start a little to the right. In a block with fewer than four controls, the spare Q-Links do nothing.

The Q-Links in Program mode

In the MPC's Program Q-Link mode the sixteen Q-Links do not follow the page. They hold this fixed set:

It moves

The two reels turn while sound comes in or the song is playing, coast to a stop about two seconds after, and lurch with the wobble. The neon grid on the page sticker rolls with them, and the sun glows with the output level. The Animation switch on the DECK page turns all movement off.

The picture shows the sound

With Visual Vibes on (DECK page, GLOBAL block), the picture on the page sticker plays like a worn video tape of what the plugin is doing:

ON THE PICTUREWHAT MOVES IT
The sun takes the Type's shade: pink for Simple, mint for VHS, orange for Hi-FiType
Snow, in four strengthsthe hiss as you hear it; in Hi-Fi it rises as the Carrier comes down
A strip of noise along the bottom, in three strengthsHead Buzz
A white streak for a momenteach dropout
A band of noise rolling up the picturethe tracking lost: Tracking in Simple and VHS, every fall to the linear track in Hi-Fi
The grid bends, in three stepsthe four wobble depths together (WOBBLE's power off straightens it)
A haze, in five stepsHi Cut below 7 kHz, thickest at 1 kHz

Visual Vibes is off in a new instance and in a project from an older version. It needs Animation on. Neither switch changes the sound, and choosing a program changes neither.

Seven read-only parameters drive the movement and the picture: Reel, Level, Snow, Head, Streak, Grid and Haze. The plugin updates them up to 20 times a second. They are not settings and you cannot automate them; leave them alone.

05／11
PATH
ＳＩＧＮＡＬ　ＰＡＴＨ　信号経路
A copy of a copy wobbles twice.

The sound goes through the machine in this order. Each box is one stage; its color says which page its controls are on.

ＴＡＰＥＷＯＢＢＬＥＮＯＩＳＥＩＮＰＵＴＤＥＣＫHQ: runs at twice the sample rate when HQ is onNoise enters at one of these two places (Position)

What the order means

  • Noise has two doors. On Pre the noise goes in at the very start and is compressed, clipped and wobbled with the music. On Post it comes in after the first wobble and stays clean.
  • The stages marked HQ are the ones that distort. With the HQ switch on they run at twice the sample rate.
  • Two wobbles. Wobble 1 is the tape. Wobble 2 is the tape after one more copy, with its own two filters behind it.
  • The Whistle comes late, after every filter and both wobbles, so it never wavers. Dropouts dip it with the rest of the sound, unless the NR playback side is on: then it comes after that, at the very end.
  • NR is in two halves. The record side sits between Tilt and Drive, the playback side just before Mono. Everything between them is the tape, and whatever the tape does there makes the playback side mistrack.
  • Breathing is not a stage. It makes the hiss rise and fall with the signal and holds the head buzz down in the pauses.
  • Hysteresis and Azimuth sit inside the VHS stage. Hysteresis replaces its tape curve, after the record level and the pre-emphasis and before the de-emphasis. Azimuth comes between the tape and the playback head, so the B-Type NR playback side hears what the tilted head lost.
  • Hi-Fi gathers the deck's faults into one place. With Type on Hi-Fi and VIBE's power on, the Hi-Fi track in the Vibe box makes the hiss, crackle, head buzz, breathing, tracking, drift and dropouts itself, and their own boxes further down rest. B-Type NR rests too.
  • Mix blends the untouched input back in at the end, delayed to line up with the tape path.

PREAMPプリアンプQ-LINK 13-16
1DRIVE
WHERE
TAPE › PREAMP · Q-Link 13
RANGE
0.0 to +24.1 dB
DEFAULT
+5.7 dB
PARAMETER
Drive

Soft clipping in the preamp, the recorder's input stage. The read-out is the gain into the clipper: the higher, the harder it pushes the sound. 0.0 dB is clean.

LISTEN FORPeaks round off and the sound thickens. Sound around -8 dBFS keeps its loudness; it lifts quieter sound and holds louder sound down.

START AT+5.7 dB is Home Recording. Subtle Glue uses +4.1 dB, Bootleg Concert +16.1 dB.

NOTEBelow about +3.1 dB (the first 17 % of the knob) the knob also blends the clean signal with the clipped one. The read-out shows only the gain, not the blend.

2TILT
WHERE
TAPE › PREAMP · Q-Link 14
RANGE
-6.0 to +6.0 dB
DEFAULT
0.0 dB
PARAMETER
Tilt

Tilts lows against highs, in front of the Drive clipper. It splits the sound at 800 Hz: turn right and the highs come up while the lows go down by the same amount; turn left for the reverse. The read-out is what the highs get; 0.0 dB is flat.

LISTEN FORTo the left, darker and heavier; to the right, brighter and thinner. With Drive up it also changes what the clipper bites on.

START ATTraining Video sits at -0.9 dB, Dream Sequence at +0.6 dB.

3SLEW
WHERE
TAPE › PREAMP · Q-Link 15
RANGE
off, then 12 to 1890 µs
DEFAULT
32 µs
PARAMETER
Slew

A slew limiter: it limits how fast the signal can move. The read-out is the shortest time the limit allows for a swing from silence to full level. Slower sound passes untouched; faster sound becomes a straight ramp. So it dulls and smears loud, bright sound and leaves quiet sound alone, which a filter cannot do.

LISTEN FORThe top end dulls and the detail smears, more on loud passages than on quiet ones.

START ATIn parentheses, how high a full-level tone passes clean. A tone 12 dB quieter passes four times as high.

  • Home Recording: 32 µs (about 5 kHz).
  • 3rd Gen Copy: 113 µs (1.4 kHz).
  • Chewed Tape: 146 µs (1.1 kHz).
  • The longest, 1890 µs: only up to 84 Hz.

NOTEFully down it reads off and the plugin skips the stage. The MPC lists the control from 0 to 100 %.

4COMP
WHERE
TAPE › PREAMP · Q-Link 16
RANGE
0 to -36 dBFS
DEFAULT
-14 dBFS
PARAMETER
Comp

A one-knob compressor with make-up gain. The read-out is the threshold; the ratio is always 4:1. Turning it up lowers the threshold and raises the make-up. Below about -12 dBFS it squashes and brings quiet sound, and noise, up.

LISTEN FORQuiet passages rise. With Position on Pre (NOISE page) the noise rises with them whenever the music stops.

NOTEAt 0 dBFS, the bottom of the knob, it compresses only peaks above full scale. Comp works in milliseconds; for a level control that works over seconds, use AGC on the DECK page.

OUTPUTアウトプットQ-LINK 9-12
5DROPOUTS
WHERE
TAPE › OUTPUT · Q-Link 9
RANGE
0 to 100 %
DEFAULT
0 %
PARAMETER
Dropouts

Short random dips, as when the tape lifts off the head. The highs go first and furthest; the lows only sag. The knob sets both how often they come and how deep they go. 0 % is off.

LISTEN FORDips of a few milliseconds in which the sound goes dull. It does not drop to silence.

START ATBad Tracking uses 15 %, Edge Damage 30 %, Chewed Tape 80 %.

NOTEFor a slow fading in and out, use Drift on the DECK page. With Type on Hi-Fi (the knob turns orange) the Hi-Fi track makes the dropouts:

  • Each one weakens the FM signal off the tape for 15 µs to 2 ms (up to 80 ms at 100 %) and brings a burst of noise and clicks.
  • A deep one makes the deck hold the sound for a moment. A long deep one sends it to the linear track for a quarter of a second.
  • How many: a good tape's 1 to 10 a minute at 6 to 18 %; 80 a minute (a poor tape after a hundred plays) at 52 %; 300 a minute at 100 %.

VIBE雰囲気Q-LINK 5-8

Saturator

The VIBE block's POWER switch. It turns the VIBE stage on or off, whichever Type you choose. Off, Split, Lows, Lo Sat, Highs, Hi Sat, Type, Azimuth and Hysteresis do nothing.

NOTEHi Cut sits in the same block but is a stage of its own: it stays in. With Type on Hi-Fi, switching VIBE off also hands the seven controls the Hi-Fi track took back to their own stages, and B-Type NR works again.

10SPLIT
WHERE
TAPE › VIBE · Q-Link 6
RANGE
200 Hz to 8 kHz
DEFAULT
2.5 kHz
PARAMETER
Split

Its job depends on Type (see The three knobs that change their name).

  • Simple: the frequency where the signal splits into a low band and a high band.
  • VHS, captioned BIAS: how well the deck is set up for the tape. The read-out says "right" at 2.5 kHz, where the knob rests. Lower (a minus percentage) is too little bias: brighter, grittier, distorting sooner. Higher (a plus percentage) is too much: duller, the highs giving way sooner. With Hysteresis on it is a real bias control, from a quarter of the right bias at the bottom to one and a half times it at the top.
  • Hi-Fi, captioned CAL: whether the playback side is set to the same level as the record side. "right" at 2.5 kHz, where the knob rests; elsewhere the read-out gives the error, from -3.0 dB at the bottom to +3.0 dB at the top. The error comes out doubled and grows with the level, so loud and quiet parts move apart or together and the sound pumps.

START ATHi-Fi - Wrong Deck has CAL at the bottom.

11LOWS
WHERE
TAPE › VIBE · Q-Link 7
RANGE
−12 to +12 dB
DEFAULT
0.0 dB
PARAMETER
Lows

In Simple: the level of the low band going into its clipper. In VHS and Hi-Fi: trims the result below 1 kHz.

12LO SAT
WHERE
TAPE › VIBE · Q-Link 8
RANGE
0 to 100 %
DEFAULT
+2.7 dB
PARAMETER
Lo Sat

Its job depends on Type.

  • Simple: how hard the low band is clipped. The read-out is the gain into the band's clipper; 0.0 dB is clean.
  • VHS, captioned REC LEVEL: the record level, from 10 dB under to 8 dB over the deck's reference level, which is at 56 %. There a tone at -8 dBFS has 3 % distortion, as on a real deck. Quiet sound comes back at the level it went in whatever the setting; what changes is how much of the loud sound the tape bends.
  • Hi-Fi, captioned REC LEVEL too: the record level, from -10 dB to +28 dB, 0 dB at the same 56 %. It decides how hard the sound meets the Hi-Fi track's hard ceiling, which a steady 1 kHz tone reaches 19 dB over reference level and a 10 kHz tone 11.5 dB over. Under the ceiling nothing distorts and the sound comes back at its own level. Turning it up also lowers the noise and the clicks against the sound.

LISTEN FORIn Hi-Fi, loud hits and held loud notes flatten against the ceiling, hard, with no softening on the way. The first milliseconds of a drum hit after silence reach it even low on the knob: the record side turns its gain up in the silence and needs 5 ms to bring it down. That is part of the format.

START ATIn Simple, 3rd Gen Copy uses +6.5 dB and Bootleg Concert +9.0 dB. In VHS, SP Tape uses 45 % and EP Tape 50 %. In Hi-Fi, Hi-Fi - Clean Deck uses 56 % (0 dB) and Hi-Fi - Hot Signal 95 % (+24.9 dB).

NOTEIn Simple, below about +1.9 dB (the first 17 % of the knob) the knob also blends the clean band with the clipped one, as Drive does.

VIBE雰囲気Q-LINK 1-4

WHERE
TAPE › VIBE · Q-Link 1
RANGE
−24 to +12 dB
DEFAULT
-3.0 dB
PARAMETER
Highs

In Simple: the level of the high band going into its clipper. In VHS and Hi-Fi: trims the result above 1 kHz.

14HI SAT
WHERE
TAPE › VIBE · Q-Link 2
RANGE
0 to 100 %
DEFAULT
+6.5 dB
PARAMETER
Hi Sat

Its job depends on Type.

  • Simple: how hard the high band is clipped. The read-out is the gain into the band's clipper; 0.0 dB is clean.
  • VHS, captioned TAPE SPEED: the tape speed, from SP (33.35 mm/s, at 0 %) through LP (16.67 mm/s, at 63 %) to EP (11.12 mm/s, at 100 %). The slower the tape, the sooner the highs give way and the lower the top of the band: 10 kHz in SP, about 6 kHz in LP, about 4.5 kHz in EP. The read-out names SP, LP and EP, the speeds of other formats inside the range (below), and gives the speed in mm/s between them.
  • Hi-Fi, captioned CARRIER: how strong the FM signal off the tape is, from 0 dB (a good tape on a good deck) down to -20 dB, 0.2 dB for every percent. Every dB lost is a dB more hiss. From about -14 dB the deck falls to the linear track now and then, more often further down, and from about -19 dB it hardly ever comes back. Carrier does not change how many clicks there are: that is Crackle's job.

LISTEN FORIn Hi-Fi, the hiss comes up, and lower down the sound drops now and then to a duller, quieter, mono version of itself with its own hiss, for about a quarter of a second each time.

START ATIn Simple, 3rd Gen Copy uses +12.5 dB and Bootleg Concert +10.2 dB. In VHS, 0 % is the SP Tape program and 100 % the EP Tape program. In Hi-Fi, Hi-Fi - Worn Rental has the carrier at -12 dB.

NOTEIn Simple, below about +1.9 dB (the first 17 % of the knob) the knob also blends the clean band with the clipped one, as Drive does. The other formats' names on the VHS read-out are labels for those speeds; the sound is the VHS tape running at that speed.

  • PAL SP (23.39 mm/s) at 32 %
  • Beta II (20.00 mm/s) at 47 %
  • PAL Beta (18.73 mm/s) at 53 %
  • Beta III (13.33 mm/s) at 83 %
  • PAL LP (11.70 mm/s) at 95 %
15HI CUT
WHERE
TAPE › VIBE · Q-Link 3
RANGE
1 kHz to 18 kHz
DEFAULT
9.0 kHz
PARAMETER
Hi Cut

A 4-pole lowpass straight after the VIBE stage. It works with every Type, and with VIBE's power off.

START ATAbout 10 kHz for a standard-speed (SP) tape, near 6 kHz for a slow-speed (EP) tape.

NOTEThe HI CUT on the WOBBLE page is a second, later filter. With Visual Vibes on, a haze comes over the picture as this one comes down below 7 kHz.

16TYPE
WHERE
TAPE › VIBE · Q-Link 4
RANGE
Simple / VHS / Hi-Fi
DEFAULT
Simple
PARAMETER
Sat Type

Chooses what the VIBE stage is.

  • Simple is a two-band saturator: it splits the signal in two and each band gets its own level and soft clip.
  • VHS is a model of the tape of a VHS deck's linear track. Quiet sound passes unchanged; loud sound loses its highs first and goes soft, the way slow tape does.
  • Hi-Fi is a model of the FM sound the rotating heads write under the picture. It stays clean up to a hard ceiling. What you hear instead is hiss that rises and falls with the music, clicks when the signal off the tape is weak, a buzz from the heads switching, and drops to the dull mono linear track when the signal is lost.

NOTEIn VHS and Hi-Fi three knobs change their meaning and caption (see the table after this page's controls). In Hi-Fi, with VIBE's power on, the Hi-Fi track also takes over Hiss, Crackle, Head Buzz, Breathing, Tracking, Drift and Dropouts, and B-Type NR does nothing. Switching Type fades the sound out and back in.

The three knobs that change their name

The Type switch in the VIBE block (three stacked buttons: SIMPLE, VHS and HI-FI) changes what the VIBE stage is, and with it what three of its knobs do.

KNOBTYPE = SIMPLETYPE = VHSTYPE = HI-FI
SPLITSplit: where the sound divides into a low band and a high bandBias: how well the deck is set up for the tapeCal: whether playback is set to the record level
LO SATLo Sat: how hard the low band is clippedRec Level: how hard the tape is drivenRec Level: how hard the sound meets the Hi-Fi track's ceiling
HI SATHi Sat: how hard the high band is clippedTape Speed: SP, LP or EPCarrier: how strong the FM signal off the tape is
LOWSLevel of the low band into its clipperTrims the result below 1 kHzTrims the result below 1 kHz
HIGHSLevel of the high band into its clipperTrims the result above 1 kHzTrims the result above 1 kHz
  • The captions, read-outs and colors change with the Type, so you can see what each knob does now and which controls the mode has taken. Each knob's entry above gives its read-outs in every Type.
  • The knobs stay. They are the same knobs on the same Q-Links, and the MPC still lists them as Split, Lo Sat and Hi Sat (the Type switch as Sat Type, VIBE's power switch as Saturator).
  • SP Tape and EP Tape show the VHS model at its two speeds. Every program whose name begins with VHS uses it too.
  • Hi-Fi does not saturate at all: it stays clean up to a hard ceiling. What gives it away is everything around the sound, below.

What Hi-Fi takes over

With Type on Hi-Fi and VIBE's power on, seven controls on other pages stop driving their own stages and drive the Hi-Fi track instead. They keep their names and places, and turn orange.

CONTROLPAGEIN HI-FI
HISSNOISEThe FM channel's noise. It rises and falls with the music by itself. 9 % at Master 0.0 dB is a real deck's.
CRACKLENOISEHow many clicks: how close the deck sits to the point where the FM signal breaks up. It does not move with Carrier.
HEAD BUZZNOISEHow badly the deck hides the switch from one head to the other. 0 % hides it as a deck does.
BREATHINGDECKThe tape played on another deck, whose playback side follows the sound its own way: it pumps.
TRACKINGDECKOne head reading weaker, and dips of the signal, one to eight head passes long.
DRIFTDECKThe signal's strength wandering slowly, up to 22 dB.
DROPOUTSTAPEShort losses of the signal: bursts of noise and clicks, holds, falls to the linear track.

B-Type NR does nothing: it belongs to the linear track.

NOISE's power and Master still work on Hiss, Crackle and Head Buzz, and Deck Power still switches Breathing, Tracking and Drift. With VIBE's power off, all seven are their own again, and Hi-Fi sounds exactly as Simple does with VIBE's power off.

The fall to the linear track

Every Hi-Fi tape also carries the mono linear track along its edge. When the FM signal gets too weak (a dip, a dropout, a low Carrier), the deck crossfades to it. The sound goes duller, 3 dB quieter and mono, with a hiss of its own, set by Hiss and twice as loud as the other Types' hiss.

The Hi-Fi sound comes back about a quarter of a second after the signal does, so each fall is a short dull, hissy patch. When the signal is lost deeper still, the deck holds the sound for a moment, fading toward silence. For fewer falls, raise Carrier, or lower Tracking, Drift or Dropouts.

Where the two tape models come from

VHS is built on the published figures of the VHS linear track: its tape speeds, its pre-emphasis, its reference level and its 3 % distortion at that level. Driven hard, it clips highs it has just lifted, and without HQ part of that folds back into the band, so keep HQ on. Hi-Fi is a real Hi-Fi deck's machinery, from the chips' datasheets, driven far out of spec. The chapter ＩＮＳＩＤＥ　ＴＨＥ　ＭＡＣＨＩＮＥ has how both work, what they measure and what is estimated.

Noise and silence

  • The effect makes noise even with no input. For a silent background, switch NOISE's power off or turn Master down to off.
  • With Position on Pre and Comp or AGC turned up, the noise swells whenever the music stops. A real recorder's level control does the same. If it is too much, turn Master down or set Position to Post.
  • A Modeled microphone adds its own noise: the capsule's hiss, or the phone line's. NOISE's power silences it; Master does not change it.

7TYPE
WHERE

PARAMETER
Mic Type

Which of the four microphones the Mic plays the sound into. On Simple each is a tone curve and nothing more; on Modeled, a real kind of microphone with the recorder it sat in.

  • Camcorder. Simple: thin and forward. Modeled: a camcorder across the room. Its level control pulls loud and quiet to one level, the hiss swells in every pause, loud hits crunch.
  • Dynamic. Simple: the widest, with a presence lift. Modeled: a stage microphone. A gentle low cut and a presence lift, nothing more.
  • Phone. Simple: narrow and nasal. Modeled: a telephone line. No bass, no top, and quiet words fade more than loud ones.
  • Boombox. Simple: dull and boxy. Modeled: a radio cassette's built-in microphone. A whisper and a shout come out at nearly one level, with tape hiss and a rounded top.

LISTEN FOROn Modeled, stop the music and the hiss and the room climb back up.

  • Boombox: over about seven seconds.
  • Camcorder: over about two and a half, or ten or more after a sound too loud for it.
  • Phone: nothing climbs, but quiet words sink further than loud ones.

START ATOn Simple, Camcorder 89 and Wedding Video use Camcorder, Answer Machine uses Phone, Bootleg Concert and Tube TV use Boombox. The five programs named Mic - ... are the same on Modeled.

NOTEChanging the type fades the mic out and the new one in. The microphones: Simple and Modeled, after this page's controls, describes each one.

8GAIN
WHERE
INPUT › MIC · Q-Link 8
RANGE
−12 to +12 dB
DEFAULT
0.0 dB
PARAMETER
Mic Gain

On Simple, the level of the microphone, after its curve. On Modeled, how loud the sound is at the microphone, as if the source were louder or closer: it comes before the microphone, so it decides how hard it drives the mic. It works only while Mic is on.

LISTEN FOROn Modeled, each microphone answers differently.

  • Camcorder: turned down, everything sits at one level and the hiss swells in the gaps. Turned up, loud sounds crunch and the hiss waits longer to come back. The level that comes out changes little.
  • Boombox: the level hardly moves, only how close the hiss sits.
  • Phone: turned down, quiet words sink.
  • Dynamic: a plain level.

START ATMic - Answer Machine uses +3 dB, Mic - Camcorder 89 and Mic - Bootleg Concert +2 dB, Mic - Wedding Video +1 dB.

NOTEThe microphone comes before AGC and the preamp, so more gain here also drives those harder. On Modeled a sound peaking at -8 dBFS counts as 104 dB SPL at the microphone; this mapping is an assumption. What each step of Mic Gain does to the Camcorder is in the chapter ＩＮＳＩＤＥ　ＴＨＥ　ＭＡＣＨＩＮＥ.

Mic Model

Which set of four microphones Mic Type chooses from.

  • Simple: each one a fixed tone curve, in stereo, with no noise of its own. Mic Gain is a level after it.
  • Modeled: microphones built from published figures: their response, how they overload, their noise, and for the Camcorder and the Boombox the level control of the recorder they sat in.

LISTEN FORSimple colors the sound and leaves its loud and quiet parts as they were. Modeled also moves them: the level controls pull them together and lift the hiss in the pauses.

START ATCamcorder 89, Answer Machine, Wedding Video, Bootleg Concert and Tube TV use Simple; the five programs named Mic - ... are the same on Modeled.

NOTEA new instance starts on Modeled; a project saved before 1.6 opens on Simple. Switching fades the mic out and the other set in.

The microphones: Simple and Modeled

The Mic plays the sound into a period microphone before the recorder hears it, as if it had been re-recorded through one. Mic Type picks one of four: Camcorder, Dynamic, Phone or Boombox. Mic Model picks the set: Simple or Modeled.

Simple

Each type is one fixed tone curve, in stereo, with no noise and no level control of its own. Projects saved before 1.6 open on Simple, and so do the five older programs with the Mic on.

TYPETHE CURVE
CAMCORDER180 Hz to 7.5 kHz, a 5 dB peak at 3.2 kHz
DYNAMIC90 Hz to 12 kHz, a 4 dB peak at 5 kHz
PHONE350 Hz to 3.4 kHz, a 6 dB peak at 1.8 kHz
BOOMBOX120 Hz to 6 kHz, a 4 dB peak at 900 Hz

Modeled

Each type is a model of one kind of microphone people recorded through in the 1980s, built from its published figures: the response, how it overloads, how much it hisses, and for the Camcorder and the Boombox the level control of the recorder it sat in. A new instance starts on Modeled, and the five programs named Mic - ... use it. The Camcorder, the Phone and the Boombox are mono, as the originals were; the Dynamic is stereo.

TYPEITS SOUNDLOUD, QUIET AND THE PAUSES
CAMCORDERA camcorder's built-in microphone, across the room: it hears the source 16 dB quieter. A low cut near 50 Hz and a soft top.Its level control holds everything from 61 to 83 dB SPL at the microphone within 1.2 dB of one level; louder than that, loud sounds and sudden onsets crunch. After a loud passage the gain comes back in about 2.5 seconds, and the hiss in the pause rises with it. After a sound louder than its range it stays down longer, ten seconds or more.
DYNAMICThe Shure 515 moving-coil stage microphone: a gentle low cut (8 dB down at 100 Hz), a 5 dB presence peak at 5 kHz, a smaller one at 8 kHz, falling away above 10 kHz.No level control: Mic Gain is a plain level.
PHONECCITT P.48, the reference telephone of the phone companies' standards body: 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz with steep edges, a carbon microphone's grit, the line's faint noise.No level control, but the carbon grows less sensitive as the sound gets quieter, so quiet words come through weaker still.
BOOMBOXA radio cassette's built-in microphone, its level control and its tape: 50 Hz to 10 kHz, with hiss.The level control turns everything from a whisper to a shout into nearly one level. After a loud passage the gain comes back over about seven seconds, and the hiss, the room and every quiet sound come up with it.

The chapter ＩＮＳＩＤＥ　ＴＨＥ　ＭＡＣＨＩＮＥ has the sources, the measurements and every estimate.

1DECK POWER
WHERE
DECK › AGC · Q-Link 13
RANGE
Off / On

PARAMETER
Deck On

Switches AGC, Drift, Tracking and Breathing off or on together, in every Type.

NOTEB-Type NR, NR Clipper, HQ, Azimuth, Hysteresis, Animation and Visual Vibes have their own switches or rest at 0; this switch leaves them alone. Init and Clean Widener switch the deck off.

2AGC
WHERE
DECK › AGC · Q-Link 14
RANGE
0 to 100 %
DEFAULT
25 %
PARAMETER
AGC

The recorder's automatic level control, in one of two kinds (AGC Model). The knob sets how much of it you hear: 100 % is the whole effect, 0 % off; on Modeled, 50 % is half of every change in dB.

  • Simple. A loud sound pulls the gain down at once; it stays down for a second and a half, then creeps back up over a few seconds and brings the background up with it, by up to 14 dB.
  • Modeled. An early VHS deck's record level circuit. Sound peaking at -8 dBFS passes at its own level. It lifts quieter sound by 9.1 dB, down to where the circuit starts to work, 10 dB below that (peaks around -18 dBFS). It cuts louder sound: every 10 dB more going in comes out only about 1 dB louder. It cuts a sudden loud sound by 10 dB in about 11 ms, and most of the rest within half a second. When it stops, the gain comes back at about 1 dB per second: after a big hit, 18 dB takes about 19 seconds.

LISTEN FORAfter a loud hit, the quiet that follows slowly swells, noise included. On Modeled it swells for far longer, and the first moments of a loud entry come through louder before the cut lands.

START AT25 % is Home Recording. Camcorder 89 uses 80 %, Wedding Video 90 %.

NOTEComp works in milliseconds; this works in seconds. On Modeled the AGC starts from full gain after a program change, the way the deck started each recording: for most of the first second, loud sound comes through lifted (the clip after Comp keeps it in bounds).

3AGC MODEL
WHERE
DECK › AGC · Q-Link 15
RANGE
Simple / Modeled
DEFAULT
Simple
PARAMETER
AGC Model

Which automatic level control the AGC knob turns up. Simple pumps: a fast duck, a pause, back up within seconds. Modeled is an early VHS deck's record level circuit, rebuilt part by part from its service manual: it ducks fast, lifts quiet sound by 9.1 dB and lets the quiet after a loud passage rise slowly, about 1 dB per second, over tens of seconds (the numbers are under AGC).

START ATTurn the AGC up on Init with the deck on to hear Modeled.

NOTEIt rests on Modeled, so Init and every program that leaves the AGC at 0 % give the Modeled one when you turn the AGC up. Every program with the AGC up, Home Recording included, uses Simple, and so does a project saved before 1.6. Switching while sound plays does not click: the new AGC settles unheard (Modeled for a second, Simple for a moment), then the sound crossfades to it in 0.1 s. The chapter ＩＮＳＩＤＥ　ＴＨＥ　ＭＡＣＨＩＮＥ takes the Modeled one apart.

Tracking

Its job depends on Type.

  • Simple and VHS: the Hi-Fi track loses lock now and then: a burst of static, a moment on the dull, quieter mono backup track, another burst, and back. More often only the right channel crackles for a moment, as it is the first to go on a real deck. Higher is more often.
  • Hi-Fi (the knob turns orange): the Hi-Fi track itself mistracks. One head reads weaker than the other, up to 4 dB at 100 %, so noise and clicks change with every head pass. The signal dips, 14 to 30 dB deep, for one to eight head passes: up to 4 dips a second at 100 %, about one every two seconds at 25 %. A deep dip brings clicks, a hold or a drop to the linear track.

START ATFresh Rental uses 6 %, Bad Tracking 65 %, Tracking Error 85 %. In Hi-Fi, Hi-Fi - Tracking Lost uses 45 %.

Its job depends on Type.

  • Simple and VHS: the Hi-Fi noise reduction at work. The hiss rises and falls with the signal, and it pushes Head Buzz down in the pauses. It needs some Hiss or Head Buzz on the NOISE page.
  • Hi-Fi (the knob turns orange): the hiss already does that by itself, so Breathing works on the music. It plays the tape on another deck, whose playback side follows the sound its own way: it reacts up to a fifth faster or slower than the record side did, and it measures the average level of the sound where the record side measured its peaks. Steady tones keep their level; moving sound pumps, by up to about 4.5 dB at 100 %.

LISTEN FORHiss that swells behind each note and sinks after it. In Hi-Fi, drums and sharp attacks lift and duck the level around them.

START ATFresh Rental uses 15 %, Hi-Fi Master 35 %, Worn Heads 45 %. In Hi-Fi, Hi-Fi - Wrong Deck uses 100 %.

B-Type NR: the four positions

NR is B-type noise reduction. The record side lifts quiet highs by up to 10 dB; the playback side cuts them again, and the hiss with them. Loud sounds pass untouched. The switch picks which sides are in.

POSITIONTHE TAPE WASWHAT YOU HEAR
OFFrecorded without, played withoutNo noise reduction.
RECrecorded with it, played withoutBright, airy, a little squashed, all the hiss.
PLAYrecorded without, played with itDull, the highs ducking in quiet passages.
ONrecorded with it, played with itOn a clean tape it only removes hiss. The more the tape has lost in between (Hi Cut, Slew, Dropouts, Drift), the more the playback side mistracks, and the duller and more unsteady the top end gets.

Wrong Switch uses REC and Stereo Rental ON; NR - Fuzz In The Gaps and NR - Blown Encoder use REC with the clipper below. The chapter ＩＮＳＩＤＥ　ＴＨＥ　ＭＡＣＨＩＮＥ takes the circuit apart.

NR Clipper: grit in the side chain

CLIPPER sits beside the NR switch. It is a clipper on the NR side chain: the control path that decides how much the NR lifts and cuts. The audio itself does not pass through it. The clipper is a pair of silicon diodes, on the record side and the playback side alike.

SETTINGWHAT IT DOES
0 %Clean. The diodes only catch sudden jumps, as the chips do; a steady tone passes untouched. A new instance starts here.
50 %The amount of every version before 1.8. A project saved with an older version loads here.
Above 50 %It drives the diodes hard, up to 30 times at 100 %. Quiet passages get dirty first, then loud ones too, and the sound gets brighter and louder.

Because it works on the side chain, the grit follows the music: it shows mostly on and around quiet passages, where the NR does the most, and changes with what goes in. It does nothing while NR is OFF, or in Hi-Fi, where the plugin ignores NR.

NR - Fuzz In The Gaps uses 80 % and NR - Blown Encoder 100 %. Wrong Switch and Stereo Rental sit at 50 %, their old sound; every other program is at 0 %.

Hysteresis: the tape's memory

The LINEAR block holds Hysteresis while Type is VHS; it needs VIBE's power on. Off, the VHS tape is the fixed tape curve. On, the tape records through a Preisach model of AC-biased recording (see ＩＮＳＩＤＥ　ＴＨＥ　ＭＡＣＨＩＮＥ). It models how tape records in general; no particular tape or deck stands behind it.

With it on, BIAS is a real bias control, from a quarter of the right bias at the bottom to one and a half times it at the top. "right" is the bias the tape is set up for.

BIASWHAT YOU HEAR
Too littleDistortion, a gate-like loss of quiet sounds and a brighter top. Near the bottom a quiet tone hardly records at all, and reverb tails vanish into the hiss.
RightThe tape as it is meant to run: about 3 % distortion at reference level, as with the tape curve.
Too muchDuller and cleaner.
  • TAPE SPEED changes the result: below half way the tape records as at SP, from there as at EP, and the change glides over about 10 ms. REC LEVEL, the emphasis and the top of the band work as they do without it.
  • It costs CPU, which is what the small bar on the ON button says: on an MPC One+ about 6.5 % of one core, against about 2.9 % with it off.
  • The sound comes about 1 ms (41.5 samples) later. The plugin reports that to the host and delays the dry signal for Mix to match.
  • Switching it crossfades over 10 ms.
  • The six programs from VHS - Factory Aligned to VHS - Six Hour Starved use it. Every other program, a new instance and a project from an older version have it off.

Azimuth: a tape from another deck

The ALIGNMENT block holds Azimuth while Type is VHS. It tilts the playback head of the linear track against the recording, from 0' to 60' (minutes of arc).

The treble cancels across the tilted head: first the very top dulls, then the top end turns hollow and notched and swishes as the tape wanders. The knob is fine at the bottom, where real tapes live: a tape from another deck is 3' to 8' off (22 to 37 % of the knob), and 60' is a head knocked out of line.

TILTKNOBSP: 3 DB DOWN / FIRST NOTCHEP: 3 DB DOWN / FIRST NOTCH

7.5'35 %6.8 kHz / 15.3 kHz2.3 kHz / 5.1 kHz
15'50 %3.4 kHz / 7.6 kHz1.1 kHz / 2.5 kHz
60'100 %850 Hz / 1.9 kHz280 Hz / 640 Hz
  • EP is three times as touchy as SP, because the tape runs three times slower.
  • With B-Type NR on ON the loss grows: the decoder takes the dulled highs for quieter ones and cuts them further.
  • At 0', where it rests, it is not there at all. Outside VHS it does nothing.
  • VHS - Borrowed Tape and VHS - Wrong Deck EP use it.

HQ

HQ runs the stages that distort at twice the sample rate: Drive, Slew, Comp, the VIBE stage, the modeled Camcorder, Phone and Boombox microphones, and the record side of B-Type NR. Hysteresis always runs at twice the rate, HQ or not.

  • Off: bright sounds that hit those stages fold back into the midrange as tones that were never played.
  • On: that is gone for highs at ordinary levels. The clippers (Drive, the Simple saturator, the Hi-Fi limiter, the VHS tape curve, Slew, B-Type NR and the Phone microphone) also smooth each step they take, so even a full-level high tone they square off folds back less, and their harmonics keep their level.
  • On takes more CPU. Switching it fades the sound out and back in.
  • HQ is on in a new instance. Choosing a program does not change it.
  • If the MPC runs short of CPU, switch Hysteresis or HQ off. Animation off also saves the work of updating the screen.
06／11
INSIDE
ＩＮＳＩＤＥ　ＴＨＥ　ＭＡＣＨＩＮＥ　内部
Somebody took the lid off and wrote down what was there.

Six parts of VHS Vibes are built from what was published about the machines: a format's own figures, a tape recording handbook's formula, the datasheets of the chips inside Hi-Fi decks, a chip's circuit diagram, the datasheets, standards and measurements behind four microphones, and a deck's service manual. A seventh, Hysteresis, is a physical model of how tape records. This chapter says what each is made of, what was measured, and what had to be estimated.

The tape itself: Type = VHS

A VHS deck without Hi-Fi records its sound on a thin track along the edge of the tape, the linear track. The tape crawls past the head at 33 mm a second, slower than an audio cassette, on a coating made for pictures. Type = VHS is a model of what that track does to sound.

The figures it is built on

FIGUREVALUEWHERE IT IS FROM
Tape speed, SP33.35 mm/sAudio Engineering Society tutorial on videotape duplication, table of audio recording formats, column VHS
Record pre-emphasis120 microseconds: the highs are lifted 6 dB per octave from 1.33 kHzthe same table
Reference level100 nWb/m, taken here as -8 dBFSthe same table
Distortion3 % third harmonic at reference levelthe same table
Top of the band, SPabout 10 kHzthe same tutorial
Biastoo much sounds dull, too little bright and distortedthe same tutorial
Tape speed, EP11.12 mm/sdeck specification sheets
Top of the band, EP4 to 6 kHzdeck specification sheets

The fourth line is the heart of it. An audio cassette reaches 3 % distortion 7 dB above its reference level and a studio machine 10 dB above. The VHS linear track is there at reference level. It has no headroom at all.

What happens to the sound, step by step

  1. Record level. REC LEVEL makes the sound louder or quieter, from 10 dB under to 8 dB over the deck's reference level.
  2. Pre-emphasis. The highs are lifted, as the format prescribes, before they reach the tape. In SP the lift starts at 1.33 kHz; a 5 kHz sound arrives at the tape about 11 dB hotter than a bass note of the same level.
  3. The tape. A smooth curve that bends more the harder it is driven and goes level at its ceiling. Its shape gives a tone at reference level 3 % third harmonic.
  4. De-emphasis. The playback side cuts the highs again, by exactly what step 2 lifted.
  5. Playback level. Playback takes off again whatever step 1 added, so the knob sets how hard the tape is driven and leaves the level of the result where it was.
  6. The top of the band. A gentle roll-off, 3 dB down at 10 kHz in SP and at 4.5 kHz in EP.
  7. Bias. A shelf that brightens or dulls the highs, depending on BIAS.

Why the highs go first

Steps 2 and 4 are exact opposites. For a quiet sound the tape in between is a straight line, so the two cancel and the sound comes back as it went in. A loud sound meets the curve with its highs already lifted. They hit the ceiling first; the lows pass under it. Step 4 then lowers what is left of them. So the louder the music, the more top it loses, while bass and voice stay.

At the slow speed everything happens at a third of the frequency: the lift starts at 440 Hz, so in EP even the midrange runs out of tape.

What comes out, measured

TESTRESULT
A quiet sound (-40 dB), SPunchanged at 100 Hz, 0.05 dB down at 1 kHz, 3 dB down at 10 kHz
A quiet sound (-40 dB), EPunchanged at 100 Hz, 3 dB down at 4.5 kHz
441 Hz at reference level, Rec Level 0 dB3.0 % third harmonic
The same tone 10 dB under reference0.3 %
The same tone recorded 8 dB over12 %, and it comes back 4.8 dB quieter
10 dB under reference, SP441 Hz loses 0.1 dB, 7 kHz loses 2.5 dB
2.5 kHz, 10 dB under referenceSP loses 0.5 dB, EP 2.3 dB
A low tone 4 dB under reference4.7 % with too little bias, 1.3 % with the bias right
6 kHz played quietly0.6 dB up with too little bias, 5.4 dB down with too much

The three knobs, in the model's terms

  • REC LEVEL is step 1. At 0 dB a tone at -8 dBFS sits exactly at the deck's reference level.
  • TAPE SPEED moves steps 2, 4 and 6 together, from SP through LP to EP.
  • BIAS at "right" does nothing. Toward too little, the tape's ceiling drops by up to 6 dB and the highs come up by up to 3 dB: bright and gritty. Toward too much, the highs lose headroom sooner and are cut by up to 6 dB: dull. With Hysteresis on, step 3 and this shelf give way to the recorder of the next section, which makes the effects of the bias itself.

What is estimated

No figures were found for EP's equalization or headroom; the model treats it as SP at a third of every frequency. Also estimated: that the lift of step 2 levels off 20 dB up, the shape of the curve beyond the 3 % point, and the sizes of the bias effects. There is no head bump: at these tape speeds it lies below 20 Hz.

Hear it

Load SP Tape and play something with cymbals and a bass line. Turn REC LEVEL up: the cymbals soften and sink, the bass stays where it was. Now turn TAPE SPEED to EP and listen to the voice go the same way. Keep HQ on while you do.

Made for pictures. It carried the music anyway.

The tape's memory: Hysteresis

The tape curve above is a fixed bend: the same level in always gives the same level out. Real tape has memory. Its coating is a crowd of tiny magnetic particles, each of which flips at a field of its own and stays flipped, so what a particle keeps depends on the fields it has already seen. A recorder works around that with bias: a strong, very high tone added to the sound, which swings the particles back and forth as the tape passes the head and fades out as the tape leaves it, leaving behind a magnetization that follows the sound. How well that works depends on how strong the bias is. Hysteresis on is a model of that process: how tape records in general, with no particular tape or deck behind it.

The model

  • The particles. A Preisach model describes them: each particle has a switching field and an interaction field, spread around the coating's coercivity.
  • The recording. Each bit of tape arrives erased, crosses the field of the record head once, with the sound and the bias carrier together, and freezes as it leaves. The bias is simulated as the real carrier, at 62.5 kHz, through a 1.5 µm head gap.
  • The depth. The coating, 3.5 µm thick, is simulated at 12 depths, each with the weaker field that reaches it. For playback they are merged into three groups, each with its own delay and playback response.
  • Offline. That simulation is far too heavy to run live. It ran in advance for 15 bias settings from 25 to 150 % of right, for SP and for EP, and the plugin stores its results as tables: for each group, what the tape keeps for each record field.
  • In the plugin. The sound, with REC LEVEL and the pre-emphasis applied, is taken to twice the sample rate. Each group reads its table with anti-aliasing (it reads the table's integral and averages the curve between samples, so the steps between them do not fold back), passes its playback response, and the three are added. A correction fitted to the simulation then takes off the highs the head's own field erases when it is driven hard. De-emphasis and the top of the band follow as without Hysteresis.

There is no live hysteretic state. The memory is in the simulation, and the tables hold its results: the plugin looks up what the simulated tape kept and holds no magnetization of its own as it plays. Between the 15 bias settings it blends the two nearest tables; a moving BIAS knob glides, the whole range in half a second at most.

What happens as the bias changes

  • Right follows a common rule: the bias at which a 6.3 kHz tone at -20 dB, in SP, has fallen 2 dB past its peak. There a 441 Hz tone at reference level comes out with 3 % third harmonic, the format's figure.
  • Too little. The bias no longer swings the particles hard enough. A quiet sound fails to flip them and hardly records: a dead zone that acts like a gate. The curve bends sooner, with odd harmonics, and the weaker bias erases less of the highs, so the top is brighter.
  • Too much. The bias swamps the signal near the gap and partly erases the highs it has just written: duller, and cleaner.
  • SP and EP have their own tables: at EP every tone is written onto a third as much tape, and the tape records it differently.

What comes out, measured

The recorder at right bias, SP, through the record and playback emphasis. Gain is level out against level in.

TONELEVEL AGAINST REFERENCEGAINTHIRD HARMONICFIFTH HARMONIC
441 Hz-20 dB+0.01 dB0.079 %0.005 %
441 Hz0 dB-0.71 dB2.93 %0.017 %
441 Hz+8 dB-4.12 dB11.4 %2.08 %
1 kHz0 dB-1.13 dB2.95 %0.096 %
  • In the whole plugin, at reference level: 441 Hz -0.74 dB and 2.91 %, 1 kHz -1.20 dB and 2.82 %; the same with HQ on within 0.05 dB.
  • BIAS swept from bottom to top in half a second under a 1 kHz tone at reference level: nothing new rises above -82 dBFS.
  • At the bottom of the knob, a 1 kHz tone under about -30 dBFS comes out some 33 dB down; by -10 dBFS it records.
  • Silence stays silent, and a tone and its negative come out as each other's negative.

Against the offline simulation, tones from 100 Hz to 10 kHz and -20 to +6 dB against reference, the output level is off by at most / on average:

SPEED25 %50 %RIGHT150 %
SP7.4 / 2.3 dB1.8 / 0.6 dB0.3 / 0.14 dB1.3 / 0.4 dB

What is estimated

  • The tape itself. The coating's thickness, the spread of its particles' switching fields, the head gap and its spacing from the tape, and the bias frequency are chosen figures for a generic tape.
  • Right bias comes from the setup rule above, and the level from the format's 3 % at reference level.
  • The correction for the highs the head erases is fitted to the simulation.
  • Held still. The tables assume the sound holds still while a bit of tape freezes. That is exact for slow sound. Well below right bias it makes the single harmonics less exact than the overall level: their error against the simulation is 5 to 8 dB on average at 25 to 50 % of right, about 1 dB at right bias.
  • All the figures above compare the plugin with the simulation, on steady tones.
Hear it

Load VHS - Factory Aligned and play something with quiet passages and reverb. Turn BIAS slowly down: the top brightens, grit comes in, and then the quiet parts start to break up and drop out. Load VHS - Whisper Gate for the bottom of the knob, then VHS - Six Hour Starved for the same fault at EP. Switch HYSTERESIS off and on to compare with the plain tape curve.

It remembers every field it ever crossed. It keeps only the last one.

The head out of line: Azimuth

The head that reads the linear track has a narrow gap that should stand exactly square across the tape. On a tape recorded by another deck it rarely does. Tilted, the gap meets one edge of the track a moment before the other, and the head hears the average of the sound over that moment. Bass does not notice. Treble whose waves are about as short as that moment cancels itself. Azimuth is that loss, on the VHS tape model.

The figures it is built on

FIGUREVALUEWHERE IT IS FROM
The loss20 log of the size of sin x / x, with x = π f W tan(a) / v: 3 dB down at 0.443 of the first notch, notches at every multiple of it, faint lobes betweena 1967 tape recording handbook
Track width W1.0 mm, the mono linear trackan excerpt of the VHS standard, quoted elsewhere
Tape speed v33.35 mm/s in SP, a third of it in EPas for Type = VHS
A well-set deck0' to 3' offworked out from the service procedure (peaking an alignment tape)
A tape from another deck3' to 8' offworked out from the tolerances; the spread is an estimate
The tilt wandering as the tape playsabout 2' peak to peak on a good professional machine; a slow wander from the tape's slitting, 0.3 to 0.9 m of tape longmeasurements of professional tape machines, borrowed

What happens to the sound

  1. The tape. Steps 1 to 3 of Type = VHS: the record level, the lift, the tape's curve.
  2. The tilted head. The sound is averaged over the time the tilt takes to cross the track: W tan(a) / v. At 7.5' in SP that is 65 microseconds.
  3. The playback side. Steps 4 to 7 of Type = VHS, and, much later, the B-Type NR decoder, which sees the dulled highs.
  4. The wander. The tilt moves by up to 1' for the knob's position plus a tenth of the tilt (2' either way at 50 %): seven parts a slow drift, 0.03 to 0.3 Hz in SP and slower in EP, three parts a faster one, 1 to 3 Hz. That is the swish.

What comes out, measured

TESTRESULT
First notch and 3 dB point against the formula, 3.75' to 60', SP, LP and EPwithin 0.5 % while the notch lies below about 8.8 kHz; within 2.5 % up to about 17.6 kHz
The response against the formula, down to -20 dB, below 20 kHzwithin 0.6 dB
The first lobe past the notch (30', SP)-13.3 dB, as the formula has it
10 kHz at SP, 5', over a minute2.9 dB down on average, swinging between 2.1 and 4.0 dB down
10 kHz at -30 dB, SP, 5', B-Type NR off / on2.9 dB down / 4.1 dB down
At 0'the stage is not there; outside Type = VHS, Azimuth at 60' changes nothing, bit for bit

What is estimated

No VHS deck's tolerance for this tilt was found, and no measurement of one tape played on many decks. The ranges for a well-set deck and for a tape from another deck are worked out from the service procedure and from tape-standard tolerances; 60' at the top of the knob is a choice, a head knocked far out of line. The wander borrows from professional machines and audio cassettes, and its two speeds and their shares are estimates.

Hear it

Load VHS - Borrowed Tape and play something with cymbals, then turn AZIMUTH back to 0' and up again: the shimmer dulls and starts to swish. Load VHS - Wrong Deck EP for the same at EP, where the first notch falls inside the band. Switch B-Type NR to ON and the top sinks further.

Two machines that never agreed on where up was.

The FM track: Type = Hi-Fi

A VHS deck marked Hi-Fi writes its sound a second way: as FM, laid deep into the tape by the spinning video heads, under the picture. It is far quieter than the linear track, and it fails in its own ways. Type = Hi-Fi is a real Hi-Fi deck's machinery, driven far out of spec, with the click amount given its own knob. At the bottom of every knob it is a deck in good order; the rest of each knob goes well past what a working deck does, because a deck in order is too clean to hear.

The figures it is built on

The VHS Hi-Fi standard itself could not be read. Its values come through the datasheets of the chips that did the work inside the decks.

FIGUREVALUEWHERE IT IS FROM
Reference level50 kHz of FM deviation at 1 kHz, taken here as a tone peaking at -8 dBFSthe chips' datasheets
Compander2:1 on record, 1:2 on playback, unity at reference levelthe chips' datasheets
Its timing5 ms attack, 70 ms recovery (one chip: 4 and 65 ms)the chips' datasheets
Its detectora peak detector, the signal weighted toward the highs (240 and 24 microseconds)one chip's datasheet and a secondary source
The emphasisa noise-reduction lift (240 and 56 microseconds) and an FM lift (56 and 20 microseconds)secondary sources, checked against the chips' figures at 10 kHz: +3.9 dB recording, -7.7 dB playback
The ceiling150 kHz of deviation, 9.5 dB over referencethe chips' datasheets
Channel noise55 dB under reference at full signal, rising 6 dB per octave; 1 dB more for every dB of signal lostthe 55 dB chosen inside the 54 to 60 dB measured on a bench; the rest is FM theory
Clicks(B / 2√3) erfc(√CNR) a second, over a band B of 300 kHzworked out from S. O. Rice's 1948 paper on FM noise; the band from a 1983 paper on VHS Hi-Fi
Head switch59.94 times a second, hidden by a 6 microsecond hold; what is left: 73 to 76 dB under a 10 kHz tonethe chips' datasheets
A weak signalthe sound held below -21 dB; the linear track after 0.3 ms below -17 dB; back after 7 to 8 turns of the head drum (233 to 267 ms)the chips' datasheets
One head weaker3 to 5 dB is within service tolerancea deck's service manual
Playback toleranceslevel within 1 to 2 dB; the expander's slope 1.93 to 2.07deck documentation; the chips' datasheets
Two decks' detectorstimes up to 20 % apart; peak or average detectors both in usesecondary sources
Dropoutscounted from 20 dB deep on the picture and from 15 microseconds; 1 to 10 a minute on a good tape, 80 on a poor one after 100 plays; the FM sound loses about half the picture's dBtape patents; the share worked out from a recording formula

What happens to the sound, step by step

  1. Record level. REC LEVEL makes the sound louder or quieter going in.
  2. The record side. A lift of the highs, then the 2:1 compressor, which halves every distance in dB from the reference level: a sound 40 dB under reference goes onto the tape 20 dB under. Then the FM lift of the highs.
  3. The ceiling. Past 9.5 dB over reference the FM deviation is cut off, hard. Through the compressor and the lifts, a steady 1 kHz tone reaches it 19 dB over reference, a 10 kHz tone 11.5 dB over. Because the compressor turns its gain up during a silence and needs 5 ms to bring it down, the first moments of a drum hit after silence reach the ceiling even with Rec Level low.
  4. The channel. What the FM receiver gives back: the sound, plus noise (HISS), plus clicks when the signal is weak (CRACKLE: each one the receiver slipping a whole cycle), plus, 59.94 times a second, the handover from one head to the other (HEAD BUZZ). The noise and the clicks follow the signal's strength: CARRIER, a small wander of its own (1 dB, never more than 3.5), DRIFT, TRACKING's dips and weaker head, and DROPOUTS.
  5. The playback side. The FM lift taken off, the CAL error, the 1:2 expander, the noise lift taken off, and the level brought back down by what step 1 added. The expander doubles every dB again, so it pushes the noise down in quiet passages and lets it up under loud ones: the hiss moves with the music without Breathing. A wrong Cal comes out doubled, and with the expander's slope off it grows with the level, so the sound pumps.
  6. A weak signal. Below -21 dB the deck holds the sound, which fades toward silence. Below -17 dB for 0.3 ms it crossfades, in 3 ms, to the linear track: the VHS tape model of the same input, in mono, at SP, 3 dB quieter, with its own hiss at twice the other Types' level. It comes back 7 to 8 drum turns after the signal does.

With every knob at rest the whole path is transparent, apart from the ceiling and a residue of the head switch 74 dB down.

What is estimated

  • Deliberately past a real deck: the top halves of Rec Level, Hiss (30 dB), Head Buzz (20 dB), Cal (its level and its slope), Crackle, Tracking, Drift and Dropouts. They are there to be heard; the bottom of each knob is the deck in order.
  • Estimates: that the ceiling cuts hard; the compander's range (30 dB either way); that the noise stops rising 10 dB under reference however weak the signal; the scale of the Carrier knob; the click margin past the first 7 % of Crackle; the signal's own small wander; the point (5 dB of carrier to noise) where the deck gives up on clicks and falls back; where the hold sits and how it fades; the 3 ms crossfade; how often, how deep and how long Tracking's dips, Drift and Dropouts are past the counted figures above.
  • Worked out rather than read: the click rate (from Rice's formula), the size of a click, the shape of what the head switch leaves.
  • Left out: the extra clicks of loud passages (not confirmed), a difference between the left and right channels' signals, the tape speed (one deck measured EP 4 dB noisier, which Carrier covers), the level control some decks had on the Hi-Fi sound (the AGC knob is a different one).
Hear it

Load Hi-Fi - Clean Deck and play something with quiet passages. Turn CARRIER down: the hiss comes up, and past about -14 dB the sound starts to drop to the dull linear track and back. Bring it back to 0 dB and turn CRACKLE up past half, then DRIFT: the clicks come in bursts at the low points. Load Hi-Fi - Wrong Deck and set CAL back to right: the pumping stops.

Clean until the signal goes. Then somewhere else entirely.

The switch on the back: B-Type NR

The linear track hisses. When stereo came to VHS, that track was split in two, each half narrower and noisier, so those decks got the B-type noise reduction of the audio cassette. B-Type NR is that circuit.

The idea

Hiss is a high sound, and you only hear it when the music is quiet. So the recorder lifts the quiet highs before they reach the tape, by up to 10 dB, and the player cuts them by the same amount afterward. The music comes back as it was. The hiss, which joined in between, has only been cut. Both sides leave loud highs alone: they cover the hiss by themselves, and lifting them would overload the tape.

The circuit

The model is the application circuit of the Signetics NE545, a chip made for this job, with the part values printed in its datasheet:

PARTVALUEWHAT IT DOES
C3015600 pFwith C302 and R301, the fixed half of the filter
C30227 nF
R3013.3 kOhm
R30247 kOhmwith C303 and F, the sliding half
C3034700 pF
F700 kOhm at rest, down to 70 Ohma resistance the circuit itself controls

The signal goes two ways. The main path passes it untouched. Beside it runs a side chain, a filter that lets only the highs through, and its output is added to the main path. That sum is the 10 dB lift.

The side chain also listens to itself. Its output is rectified into a control voltage, and that voltage turns F down. As F conducts, the filter's corner slides upwards, so less and less passes: the louder the highs, the less is added, until at the circuit's reference level nothing is. This is the sliding band.

The control voltage has two speeds. It follows the music with a time of about 100 ms, slow enough not to distort the sound. A sudden loud sound would get through boosted before that, so for a large jump the time drops to about 2 ms, and a clipper in the side chain, a pair of silicon diodes, holds the overshoot down for the instant in between.

The player is the same side chain turned around: connected in a loop, subtracting from the signal where the recorder added.

Solved exactly

A loop of this kind is hard to compute, because the output depends on a filter whose setting depends on the output. The model solves the whole network for every sample, with its two capacitor charges and with F included, so nothing in the loop lags by a sample. As a result the playback side undoes the record side almost perfectly when nothing lies between them: on music, what remains is about 130 dB below the signal.

Against the datasheets

The datasheets of the NE545 and of a second chip of the same kind, the TEA0665, give the record side's lift at eight points. Three things they do not give as numbers (one amplifier's gain, another's rise with frequency, and how F follows the control voltage) were fitted to those eight points.

TONELEVEL UNDER REFERENCEDATASHEETMODEL
1.4 kHz20 dB+4.4 dB+4.3 dB
1.4 kHz30 dB+7.5 dB+7.6 dB
2 kHz25 dB+7.0 dB+7.2 dB
5 kHz20 dB+3.2 dB+2.9 dB
5 kHz30 dB+8.2 dB+7.9 dB
5 kHz40 dB+10.3 dB+10.3 dB
10 kHz20 dB+2.6 dB+2.9 dB
10 kHz30 dB+6.5 dB+6.8 dB

The chips themselves are specified to 2 dB.

Other things measured on the model:

  • Very quiet sound is lifted 0.6 dB at 200 Hz, 3.7 dB at 600 Hz, 9.3 dB at 2.4 kHz and 10.3 dB at 5 kHz.
  • At reference level the lift is under 0.2 dB.
  • Hiss at 8 kHz, through the playback side alone, drops by 10.5 dB.
  • A sudden jump from quiet to reference level overshoots by 0.9 dB and has settled within 5 ms. After the loud sound stops, the full lift is back in about 155 ms.

Two values are estimates: the level at which the fast smoothing takes over, and the shape of the diodes' curve. The model takes the circuit's reference level as -8 dBFS, the same level the VHS tape model takes as the deck's.

The clipper: NR Clipper

The CLIPPER knob sets where the diodes start to conduct, on the record side and the playback side alike.

SETTINGMEASURED
0 %1 kHz at the NR's reference level: under 0.001 % distortion. 10 kHz 10 dB over it: under 0.3 %, inside the chips' specification. A sudden jump is still caught.
50 %The amount of every version before 1.8, which used a hard clamp: the third harmonic of 1 kHz at reference level within 0.3 dB of it, its hold on a jump within 0.01 dB. The diodes' knee is round, so it starts lower down: a tone 10 dB under reference level has 3.1 % where the clamp had 1.1 %.
100 %The side chain driven 30 times harder into the diodes: a loud 1 kHz tone about 10 % distortion. Brighter and louder as well.

The clipper sits in the side chain, so the circuit around it shapes what it does: you hear it where the side chain is busiest, on quiet highs and the moments around them.

Why it mistracks

The playback side decides how much to cut from the level it sees. If the tape gives back less than was recorded, it sees a quieter sound than the recorder did, takes it for one that was lifted more, and cuts more. So it makes every loss of the tape larger.

BETWEEN THE TWO SIDESWITHOUT NRWITH NR ON BOTH SIDES
The tape plays 2 dB quiet (5 kHz, 30 dB under reference)2 dB down4.3 dB down
The tape has lost its highs from 4 kHz (8 kHz, 25 dB under reference)6.5 dB down12.2 dB down

In the plugin everything from Drive to Dropouts lies between the two sides. So with NR on ON, Hi Cut, Slew, the VIBE stage, Drift and Dropouts all become stronger in the highs, and unsteady, because the cut moves with the music. That is the sound of a worn tape in a deck with the switch on.

What it means for the knobs

  • It works on quiet highs. Sound near -8 dBFS and above passes almost untouched on both sides. To hear NR, play something with quiet passages, or turn the input down.
  • Hiss is only reduced if it is on the tape. With the noise's Position on Post, the hiss joins between the two sides and ON or PLAY cuts it. With Position on Pre it goes in before the record side, is lifted and cut like the music, and comes out as loud as before.
  • REC alone is the lift without the cut: bright, airy, a little squashed, because quiet highs come up and loud ones do not.
  • PLAY alone is the cut without the lift: dull, and duller the quieter it gets.
Hear it

Load Wrong Switch, a tape recorded with the switch on and played with it off, and compare it with NR on OFF. Then load Stereo Rental, with NR on both sides of an aged tape, and switch NR between ON and OFF during a quiet passage: the top end ducks and comes back with the music.

Built to take something away. Set wrong, it adds.

Four microphones: Mic Model = Modeled

This section is about the Modeled set; the INPUT page lists the Simple curves. Each of the four types is built from published figures for one kind of microphone of the period. Where a figure was missing, the value is an estimate, and the text below says so.

One level for all four

A microphone overloads and hisses at a sound pressure, and a plugin only has digital levels, so the stage has to decide how loud a digital level is in the air. It takes a sound peaking at -8 dBFS, the level the rest of the plugin treats as the recorder's reference, to be 104 dB SPL: a loud voice close to the microphone, or a band heard from the crowd. 94 dB SPL (1 pascal), the pressure microphones are specified at, then peaks at -18 dBFS.

This mapping is an assumption. No document can fix it for a plugin. It was chosen so that the electret's documented overload lies 6 dB above reference: music played in at reference level passes cleanly, and Mic Gain +6 dB reaches the overload. The same mapping serves all four types, and every type's response is 0 dB at 1 kHz. Mic Gain moves the sound along it, as a louder or a closer source would.

The Camcorder stands further off. The model puts its camera across the room, 16 dB further from the source than a close microphone (about six times the distance in free field), so it hears everything 16 dB quieter, before Mic Gain's own change.

Its level control works from 60.8 to 82.8 dB SPL at the microphone. With the distance, that is -35 to -13 dBFS peak coming in at Mic Gain 0. Here is what Mic Gain does to ordinary material: music at -18 dBFS rms, and a sine at that level.

  • -12 to -6 dB: inside the range. Loud and quiet parts 15 dB apart come out 3 to 4 dB apart (3 dB at -12). In a 2 s gap the hiss rises to within 28 dB of the loud part.
  • 0 dB: at the top of the range. The sine sits 1.8 dB inside it, with 0.28 % distortion; a tone peaking at -12 dBFS sits 1.2 dB past it. The music's loud passages hold the level control at its lowest, so they keep their 15 dB over the quiet ones, with a little crunch: the peaks come out 0.5 dB lower against the rest. The hiss in the gap is 54 dB under, and comes up some seconds after the music stops (7 seconds after this music).
  • +6 to +12 dB: past the range. Loud sounds crunch. The sine has 0.7 % distortion at +6 dB and 3.1 % at +12 dB; the music's peaks come out 4 to 9 dB lower against the rest, and at +12 the loud and quiet parts are 13 dB apart. The hiss in the gap is 64 dB under, and the gap stays quiet for about 22 seconds before it comes up.

Mic - Camcorder 89 (Mic Gain +2 dB) and Mic - Wedding Video (+1 dB) put that -12 dBFS tone 3 and 2 dB past the top of the range: squashed, with a little crunch (0.6 and 0.5 % distortion).

Each one, step by step

Camcorder

A camcorder's built-in microphone was a decent electret. What gave its sound away was the record chain behind it: a mic amp, then a level control with a great deal of fixed gain in front of a short range. The model follows the JVC GR-C1's chain. It is mono: one built-in microphone, one audio track, so left and right are summed first.

  1. The distance. The source is heard 16 dB quieter: a camera across the room.
  2. The capsule. The electret's highs: one peak filter gives the WM-61A's rise, flat to 5 kHz, a little up at 8 kHz, about 2.5 dB up around 15 kHz. Its low cut: the capsule and the gate of its transistor form a first-order low cut at 53 Hz. Its self-noise: white noise at 26 dB SPL(A). Its overload: the transistor gives way gently above 110 dB SPL, the negative half of the wave first, reaching 1 % distortion there, second harmonic as well as third.
  3. The mic amp's band. A second-order low cut and a first-order top cut, fitted to the TRV900's measured microphone input: 3 dB down at 50 Hz on top of the capsule's own cut, and a soft top, 1.7 dB down at 10 kHz and 3.6 dB at 15 kHz.
  4. The mic amp's overload. Both halves alike, 1 % distortion at 107 dB SPL: the level at which the two datasheets' microphone amplifiers reach their maximum output with this capsule. It gives way before the capsule's transistor does.
  5. The ALC. A fixed record gain of 42 dB. The camera's nominal microphone level, -66 dBs, serves as the knee: from this capsule that is 60.8 dB SPL at the microphone, -35 dBFS peak coming in at Mic Gain 0, and the gain brings it to 1.2 dB under reference. Above the knee a peak detector on the output turns the gain down by 18 dB for every dB it sees: 22 dB of input give 1.2 dB of output, so the end of the range, 82.8 dB SPL, comes out at reference. There the gain has come down by 20.8 dB, as far as it goes; past it the output follows the input up again.
  6. The gain element's distortion. The Boombox's, after the ALC: 0.3 % at the end of the range, rising quickly past it.

The level control's timing is an estimate. No camcorder of the period has its ALC's time constants in a document that could be read: the JVC's are on its schematic, but not legibly.

  • Attack. The detector charges with 20 ms, slower than the Boombox's, because a camcorder's level control is reported to let a sudden loud sound distort before it reacts.
  • Recovery. It discharges with 19 seconds, which brings the gain back at 8.2 dB a second, the whole 20.8 dB in about 2.5 seconds. That is faster than the Boombox, because the Sanyo manual says the recovery is shortened for the microphone, and slow enough for the "several seconds" reviewers describe.
  • After a sound louder than the range, the detector holds more than it needs and the gain stays at its lowest until that has drained away. At Mic Gain 0 the gain starts back 2 seconds after the -12 dBFS tone stops and 7 seconds after the music; at +12 dB, 22 to 24 seconds after.

There is no mechanism noise. A camcorder's microphone does pick up its own motors, the makers say so, but no level or spectrum was found for it. The only noise is the capsule's, and the ALC lifts it in every pause: 17 dB down right after a sound in its range, then up with the gain, to the full 42 dB of record gain.

Dynamic

Four filters fitted to the twelve read points: a gentle low cut, the presence peak, the smaller peak above the dip at 6.5 kHz, and the fall above 10 kHz. A moving coil does not overload at these levels and its own noise is far below a recorder's, so there is neither. There is no proximity lift: the guide gives it only at 1 cm, and no distance in between is documented.

Phone

  1. The carbon's sensitivity. Below reference level a carbon microphone grows less sensitive the quieter the sound: here by a quarter of a dB for every dB, by 10 dB at most.
  2. Its distortion. A second harmonic of 3 % at reference level.
  3. The reference telephone. Eight filters fitted to all 24 points of the P.48 table: the steep low cut, the broad rise to 2.5 to 3 kHz, and the cliff above 3.4 kHz.
  4. The line. Noise at -65 dBm0 in the band from 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz.

A phone line carries one channel, so the Phone sums left and right before step 1 and is mono.

Boombox

  1. The capsule. The Camcorder's electret, its step 2 above, and only one: the built-in microphone of a radio cassette is mono, so the Boombox sums left and right first.
  2. The ALC. A fixed record gain of 37 dB brings the bottom of the ALC's range (-60 dBm from the capsule, 66.8 dB SPL, -45 dBFS here) up to reference level. Above it, a peak detector on the output turns the gain down by 14 dB for every dB it sees above reference: 45 dB of input give 3 dB of output, to the end of the range 45 dB up. The detector charges within milliseconds and lets go through 22 uF and 1 MOhm: a time of 22 seconds, of which the loop needs only the first third, so the gain comes back at 5.5 dB a second.
  3. The gain element's distortion. 0.5 % at the level of the LA3220's measurement, a little less at the start of the range.
  4. The tape. Its hiss, 45 dB under the level the ALC records at, and its band, 50 Hz to 10 kHz.

  • The level mapping above.

The ALC's knee is hard; the TRV900's is soft, so just above the knee the model comes out up to 1.7 dB lower than that camera.
