For the line noise: the limit taken as the level, the reference junction taken as 0 dBr in 600 Ohm, the band edges as gentle ones, no psophometric weighting.
  • Boombox: the ALC's attack (no charging current is published): 5 ms; that its range starts at the capsule level the WM-61A's sensitivity gives; that it starts where the output reaches -8 dBFS; the cassette's band edges taken as -3 dB points; its hiss measured in that band without weighting.
  • Left out, for want of figures: a camcorder's wind filter, its motor noise, how a microphone's housing colors it, the proximity effect at ordinary distances, the carbon's own noise, and the 8-bit coding of digital phone lines.
Hear it

Load Mic - Bootleg Concert and stop the music: within seconds the hiss and the room climb up as the ALC lets go, and the next note slams them down. Load Mic - Answer Machine and play a voice that goes from loud to soft: the soft words sink further than they should. In Mic - Camcorder 89, turn MIC GAIN up and listen to kicks and loud chords crunch; stop the music and, some seconds later, the hiss and the room come up behind the camera's level control. For the Dynamic, choose Init, switch the Mic on and pick it: a presence lift, nothing more.

The cheapest part in the machine, and the nearest to the sound.

The deck's level control: AGC Model = Modeled

In an early VHS deck an automatic gain control set the record level. AGC Model = Modeled is the record level circuit of one early VHS deck, rebuilt from its service manual: the schematic, the parts list and the description of the circuit. The AGC entry on the DECK page describes the Simple AGC.

The circuit

The deck's audio chip has a gain element at its input and an output amplifier after it. The output does two jobs: it is the deck's audio out, and it feeds a detector that sets the gain. So the control is a loop: the detector hears the output, after the gain has already turned it down.

PARTVALUEWHAT IT DOES
C704.7 uFcouples the output into the detector
R1031 kOhmin series with C70
R10422 kOhmto ground: the path that lets C70's charge drain
D21germanium diodepasses the positive half of the wave only
C8047 uFholds the rectified peak: its voltage sets the gain
R107 + R1081.2 MOhm + 560 kOhmdrain C80 slowly; their junction carries the control voltage to the chip
C810.01 uFat the control input: a lag of 3.8 ms
a switchshorts C80 in playback, so every recording starts at full gain

The values come from the schematic, checked against the parts list.

How it moves

Down, in two steps. When a loud sound arrives, C70 and C80 charge together through the diode. C70 is ten times smaller, so it fills ten times faster and then blocks: within a few cycles C80 has taken about 9 % of the excess. Because the gain law is steep, that alone is a cut of 10 dB or more, reached in about 11 ms. The rest follows as C70's charge drains through R104, over about half a second.

Back up, slowly. When the sound stops, the diode stops conducting, and C80 can only drain through R107 and R108. That takes over a minute to empty it, and the gain comes back at about 1 dB per second. Nothing holds the gain down on purpose; the slow drain does it.

The gain law and the levels

The chip's own datasheet was not found. The replacement part's datasheet gives two points at 1 kHz: 0.55 V out for 0.25 mV in, and 0.8 V out for 25 mV in, "AGC 40 dB". That is 40 dB more input for 3.25 dB more output, about 12 : 1. It gives no curve and no timing.

So the model takes the simplest law that meets those points: above a knee, the gain falls in a straight line in dB as C80's voltage rises (as a transistor junction used as a variable resistance would make it), down to at most 40 dB. Two numbers of that law were fitted on the circuit itself, with a steady 1 kHz tone: where it starts (0.769 V on C80) and how steep it is (88.3 dB per volt).

The level comes from the service manual's adjustment: the reference input is set to give 2.2 V peak to peak at the output, 1.1 V peak. The plugin takes its reference level, a peak of -8 dBFS, to be that input.

Where the knee lies is not printed. The manual's adjustment procedure checks a tone 10 dB below the reference and expects it back near full level, which only works if the AGC is already at work there. So the model puts the knee 10 dB below the reference, peaks of about -18 dBFS.

In the plugin

  • Stereo. The deck was mono. The detector hears the louder of the two channels, and both get the same gain.
  • Unity at reference. At the reference level the circuit cuts by 9.1 dB. The plugin lifts everything by that much, so a steady tone peaking at -8 dBFS passes at its own level, quieter sound comes up by 9.1 dB, and louder sound is cut.
  • The knob. The detector always works on the circuit's full gain, so its timing never changes. The knob sets how much of its gain change you hear, in dB: at 50 % half of it, at 0 % none, and then the plugin skips the stage.
  • The start. C80 is empty after a program change, as the deck's was at the start of each recording. For most of the first second, loud sound comes through lifted.

What comes out, measured

A 1 kHz tone, AGC at 100 %.

TESTRESULT
A steady tone at the knee, 10 dB under referenceno cut: lifted by 9.08 dB
At referencecut by 9.08 dB: out at its own level
10 dB over referencecut by 18.23 dB (the circuit simulated alone: 18.2)
30 dB over reference, 40 dB over the kneecut by 36.75 dB: 3.25 dB louder out, as the datasheet gives
A jump of 20 dB from the knee10 dB of cut after 10.9 ms, 13.0 dB after 50 ms, 17.6 dB after half a second (of 18.2)
After that sound stopsthe gain comes back at 0.98 dB per second; all of it in about 19 seconds
From rest, a tone at referencewithin 1 dB of its level after 0.85 s

What is estimated

  • The gain law: its shape. Only the two datasheet points are known; the straight line in dB is an assumption, and its steepness and starting point follow from it and from where the knee is put.
  • Where the knee lies: 10 dB under the reference, read from the adjustment procedure. The evidence is not all one way, and anything from 20 dB under the reference to the reference itself is possible.
  • The diode: as a germanium diode, 0.15 V and 100 Ohm; the resistance of the chip's output, 100 Ohm; that the output clips at 4.5 V either side (it decides only how hard a sudden loud sound charges the detector).
  • The control range: 40 dB, the datasheet's test condition. The datasheet gives no maximum.
  • That the chip's gain follows its control input at once. Only C81's lag is in the model.
  • Left out, for want of figures: any leakage of the germanium diode and any current drawn by the chip's control input, which could only make the recovery faster (up to about 2.5 dB per second); any load on the audio output that would speed up the second step of the attack.
Hear it

Choose Init, switch Deck Power on, set AGC to 100 % and AGC Model to Modeled. Play a drum loop with a quiet break: the AGC holds the hits down, and in the break the room and the hiss rise slowly, a dB a second, long after a Simple AGC would have come back. Then set AGC to 50 % for half of that.

It listened to itself. It took a long time to forget.
07／11
SWITCHES
ＳＷＩＴＣＨＥＳ　スイッチ
One click, and a small red light in the dark.

Every section of the machine has its own switch, so you can take a part out without touching its knobs. These are all of them.

SWITCHPAGE, BLOCKDEFAULTWHAT IT DOES
MONOTAPE › OUTPUTOffSums left and right into one, near the end of the path: only Mix and Output come after it.
POWERTAPE › VIBEOnThe VIBE block's POWER switch. It turns the VIBE stage on or off, whichever Type you choose. Off, Split, Lows, Lo Sat, Highs, Hi Sat, Type, Azimuth and Hysteresis do nothing.
POWERWOBBLE › WARPOnThe WOBBLE page's POWER switch. It turns both wobbles and Scrape off or on together. The two filters of this page stay in.
POWERNOISE › NOISEOnThe NOISE page's POWER switch. It turns all noise off or on: Hum, Buzz, Head Buzz, Hiss, Crackle, Whistle and the modeled microphones' own noise.
POWERINPUT › CHORUSOffSwitches the chorus on or off: a short modulated delay near the start of the path, with left and right out of phase for width.
POWERINPUT › MICOffPlays the sound into one of four period microphones before it reaches the recorder, as if it had been re-recorded through one. Mic Model chooses which set of four. The mic fades in and out when switched.
DECK POWERDECK › AGCOnSwitches AGC, Drift, Tracking and Breathing off or on together, in every Type.
ANIMATIONDECK › GLOBALOnThe moving reels, grid and sun on or off. It is also the master switch of Visual Vibes. Off saves the work of updating the screen.
VISUAL VIBESDECK › GLOBALOffThe picture shows the sound. The picture on the page sticker behaves like a worn video tape playing what the plugin is doing: the sun in the Type's own shade, snow that thickens with the hiss, a strip of noise with Head Buzz, a white streak at each dropout, a rolling band when the tracking is lost, the grid bending with the wobble, and a haze as Hi Cut comes down.
HQDECK › GLOBALOnRuns the stages that distort (Drive, Slew, Comp, the VIBE stage, the modeled microphones and the record side of B-Type NR) at twice the sample rate, so bright sounds that hit them do not fold back into the midrange as tones that were never played.

Animation, Visual Vibes and HQ are not part of the programs: choosing a program leaves them as you set them.

What a switch leaves in

  • VIBE's power off: Hi Cut stays in. With Type on Hi-Fi, the seven controls the Hi-Fi track had taken go back to their own stages, and B-Type NR works again.
  • WOBBLE's power off: the two filters of the WOBBLE page stay in.
  • Noise off: silences every noise, the Whistle, the head-switching buzz and the modeled microphones' own noise included. In Hi-Fi it also silences the FM channel's noise, clicks and head switch, and the linear track's hiss; the holds and the falls to the linear track stay, as they are part of the deck.
  • Deck Power off: AGC, Drift, Tracking and Breathing stop, in every Type. B-Type NR, NR Clipper, HQ, Azimuth, Hysteresis, Animation, Visual Vibes and Dropouts keep working.
  • Animation off: Visual Vibes shows nothing either.

47VHS - Factory AlignedHysteresis on, with the bias right: an SP tape on a deck set up at the factory, recorded a little under reference level. Close to SP Tape.
48VHS - Bias DriftHysteresis on, the bias drifted a third of the way down: a brighter top and a little grit on the quiet parts.
49VHS - Starved BiasHysteresis on, the bias near the bottom: soft passages break up, loud ones come through.
50VHS - Whisper GateHysteresis on, almost no bias: a quiet tone hardly records at all, so tails and reverb break off, leaving only the hiss.
51VHS - Hot And StarvedHysteresis on, too little bias and recorded hot: gritty quiet parts and squashed peaks.
52VHS - Six Hour StarvedVHS - Six Hour Tape with Hysteresis on and too little bias: at EP the highs dull themselves as well.
53NR - Fuzz In The GapsWrong Switch with less hiss and NR Clipper at 80 %: a bright fuzz that swells in the gaps and ducks under the loud hits.
54NR - Blown EncoderNR Clipper at 100 %, recorded with noise reduction into a hot VHS tape: the harshest pairing.

Five recipes

  • A deck with the bias set wrong: set Type to VHS, switch HYSTERESIS on and turn BIAS down. Or start from VHS - Bias Drift.
  • A slow-speed (EP) tape: set Hi Cut near 6 kHz, Lo Cut near 100 Hz and raise Hiss. Or set Type to VHS and turn TAPE SPEED to EP.
  • A standard-speed (SP) tape: Hi Cut about 10 kHz, Lo Cut about 50 Hz. Or set Type to VHS with TAPE SPEED at SP.
  • A clean Hi-Fi sound: start from Hi-Fi - Clean Deck. Or keep the wobbles and the noise low on any Type: the rotating heads have no wow or flutter to speak of.
  • A tape from another deck: set Type to VHS and turn AZIMUTH to 3' to 8'.

NOTES
ＮＯＴＥＳ　ノート
In pencil, on the inside of the sleeve.

How it behaves

  • Turning a wobble knob while sound plays. A wobble depth or rate changes the plugin's own delay. The plugin follows a small move at a limited pace, so the pitch bends by a couple of percent at most. After a big jump, once the knob rests, the sound crossfades to the new delay in 25 ms (a brief blur) and the bend is over.
  • Timing. The wobble delays hold the sound back by their resting length, a few milliseconds on most programs. HQ adds about 3 samples and Hysteresis about 1 ms. The plugin reports the total to the host as its latency, half a second after it stops changing, so a host that compensates keeps the track in time.
  • Skipped stages. The plugin skips any stage whose amount is zero.

What comes from real machines

FROM VCR MANUALS AND SERVICING BOOKSIN THE PLUGIN
The heads switch once per video field, 59.94 times a second, and the join is audible as a buzz on high notes.Head Buzz
A Hi-Fi deck that loses its carrier makes static and falls back to the mono linear track. The right Hi-Fi channel fails before the left.Tracking
Camcorder level controls duck fast, hold for seconds and creep back up.AGC
Hi-Fi noise reduction breathes: 5 ms up, 70 ms back.Breathing
A dropout is the tape lifting off the head, which costs the highs far more than the lows.Dropouts
The line whistle of a TV set sits at 15.734 kHz.Whistle

This is what Head Buzz, Tracking, Breathing and the others do in Simple and VHS. No figures were found for their other times and depths, which are set by ear. The parts built from published figures are in the chapter ＩＮＳＩＤＥ　ＴＨＥ　ＭＡＣＨＩＮＥ.

10／11
OLD TAPES
ＯＬＤ　ＴＡＰＥＳ　互換性
Nothing you recorded is lost. It only waits.

Will your old project sound the same? Almost always, yes. A project made with an older version loads with every setting in place, and one saved with 1.3 to 1.7 sounds as it did. Every new control starts where it changes nothing, and every older program is unchanged. The few exceptions are below.

The exceptions

  • HQ with a modeled microphone or B-Type NR (projects from before 1.7). HQ now also covers the modeled microphones and the record side of B-Type NR. The false tones they used to fold back into the midrange are gone; level and tone stay. The programs that use them stay within a third of a dB of 1.6 below 10 kHz. Nothing to do.
  • HQ on, with a clipper driven hard (projects from before 1.8). With HQ on, Drive, the Simple saturator, the Hi-Fi limiter, the VHS tape curve, Slew, B-Type NR and the Phone microphone now smooth each step they take, and the filters around them are steeper. You get fewer fold-back tones and the same harmonics. Sound below the clipping is unchanged. Nothing to do.
  • Hi-Fi with HQ on (projects from 1.7). The hiss is 1.3 to 2 dB quieter than it was, and Crackle and Head Buzz 0.5 to 1 dB quieter (up to 3 dB with Breathing up). All three are now as loud as with HQ off. Raise them a little if you miss it.
  • HQ on (projects from before 1.8). The sound comes about 1.7 samples later than in 1.7. The plugin tells the host, so nothing to do.
  • Whistle above 60 % (projects from before 1.7). It is louder now, by up to 15 dB at 100 %. Turn it down if it screams too much. Up to 60 % it is unchanged.
  • B-Type NR (projects from before 1.8). Its side-chain clipper is now a diode curve, a soft knee where 1.7 had a hard clamp. The project loads with NR Clipper at 50 %, the old amount, and differs only slightly, about 35 dB below the sound. Nothing to do.
  • Type automation recorded in 1.5 or 1.6. It stores only a knob position, and Type gained a third position in 1.7, so the old VHS position now reads as Hi-Fi. Set the automation to VHS again. The project's own Type setting stays as it was.

With HQ off, none of the HQ items apply. With NR off, the B-Type NR item does not apply.

Where an older project starts

  • New controls start where the plugin sounds as it did without them: Scrape and Whistle at 0 %, B-Type NR at Off, Type at Simple, Azimuth at 0', Visual Vibes and Hysteresis off, NR Clipper at 50 %.
  • Mic Model and AGC Model open on Simple in a project saved before 1.6, the microphones and the AGC it was made with. A new instance starts both on Modeled.
  • HQ keeps the project's setting. A project saved before HQ existed opens with it off. A new instance has it on.
  • NR Clipper starts at 0 % in a new instance.

The programs

Every older program sounds as it did and keeps its number: newer programs come after Init and after each other. No older program uses the newer controls. The five with the Mic on keep the Simple microphones, and every program with the AGC up, Home Recording included, keeps the Simple AGC.

Credits

VHS Vibes 1.8.0, by anthonytheinventor.

Inspired by the idea of James Peck's "VHS Audio Degradation Suite" for Reaktor: the order of the stages and what each one is for. All code is original. VHS Vibes takes nothing from the Reaktor ensemble and uses no samples: it synthesizes every noise.
